ideaBrief.title: Crisis Command: IT Risk Protocol
ideaBrief.coreMetaphor: Students run a project war room and stop risks before they damage the project.
ideaBrief.successVision: Students learn to classify risks, choose responses, and explain their choices.

state.problemStatement: In COM0463, many students treat the risk register as a form to fill in. In a class of 40 students, only about 45% take part actively in static risk tasks, and the average risk-analysis score is about 65/100. Students often confuse likelihood and impact. This game makes risk choices visible through project health, budget, and event logs.
state.targetPopulation: 40 final-year COM0463 IT Project Management students.
successCriteria: Improve Bloom L4 analysis scores by 30%.

bloomOutcomes.outcome: Explain the difference between likelihood and impact.
Analyse why a mitigation choice worked or failed.
Evaluate a set of risk responses.

state.narrativeTheme: Crisis Command puts students in a software project war room. A launch is close, and risks keep appearing. Students must classify each risk and choose a response before project health falls. Self-Determination Theory supports choice, feedback, and teamwork. Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics connects risk cards to pressure and a war-room feeling. Bloom Taxonomy guides learning from basic terms to a final risk register. Kirkpatrick four-level evaluation checks reaction, learning, transfer, and results. Tusler risk categories help students name and compare threats.
state.gameOverview: Students inspect risk cards, choose responses, spend budget, and watch project health change. After play, they review the event log and write a short risk report.
state.sdtAutonomy: Students choose which risks to accept, prevent, transfer, or respond to.
state.sdtCompetence: Students get quick feedback after each choice and improve over rounds.
state.sdtRelatedness: Students discuss decisions and compare strategies during the debrief.

rewardStructure.elite: Top students earn a Crisis Strategist badge.
rewardStructure.professional: Students who meet the target earn a Risk Analyst badge.
rewardStructure.access: All students receive the debrief report and practice cards.

mdaAnalysis.mechanics: Risk cards, budget tokens, event logs, timers, and project health meters.
mdaAnalysis.dynamics: Students feel pressure because ignored risks create later problems.
mdaAnalysis.aesthetics: The game should feel like a focused project war room.

scenarios.title: Server Failure
scenarios.setup: A major server risk triggers during launch week.
scenarios.loseCondition: If health falls below 50%, losePoints=0 and the result becomes a debrief case.
scenarios.outcome: Students learn why high-impact risks need early action.

scenarios.title: Vendor Delay
scenarios.setup: A supplier delay threatens the project schedule.
scenarios.winCondition: Student chooses a response that protects the critical path.
scenarios.loseCondition: If the schedule slips, losePoints=0 and the class reviews the missed signal.
scenarios.outcome: Students compare probability, impact, and timing.

scenarios.title: Scope Creep
scenarios.setup: A stakeholder requests extra features during a risky sprint.
scenarios.winCondition: Student protects scope and spends budget on the highest risk.
scenarios.loseCondition: If budget runs out, losePoints=0 and the failure is discussed safely.
scenarios.outcome: Students connect scope pressure with risk response.

gamePhases.name: Choose
gamePhases.description: Pick a response and spend budget.

gamePhases.name: Resolve
gamePhases.description: See the result and event log.

frs.description: System shall let students classify risks by likelihood and impact.
System shall track project health, budget, and schedule pressure.
System shall log each choice, event, score change, and reflection in an audit event record.

nfrs.desc: The game should react quickly during class.
Students should understand the first task quickly.

nfrs.target: GDPR and KVKK aware log handling

nfrs.desc: The interface should be readable and keyboard friendly.
The session should not lose progress during normal use.

state.gameDuration: 75 minutes: briefing, play rounds, risk autopsy, and final reflection.

sessionSteps.name: Briefing
sessionSteps.description: Instructor explains terms and shows one example risk.

sessionSteps.name: Risk rounds
sessionSteps.description: Students classify risks and choose responses.

sessionSteps.name: Crisis events
sessionSteps.description: The system triggers events from ignored risks.

sessionSteps.name: Debrief
sessionSteps.description: Students review logs and improve the risk register.

state.logPrivacy: The system logs choices, events, scores, and reflections. Logs use course pseudonyms. Shared reports do not show private student data.
state.dataCollectionPlan: Data comes from pre/post quizzes, event logs, reflections, and the final risk report. The instructor uses it for feedback and grading.

tuslerRisks.mitigation: Use early code review and reserve budget for serious technical risks.
tuslerRisks.preventive: Run a technical debt check before crisis rounds.

tuslerRisks.mitigation: Prepare a backup plan for rare but severe class or system failures.
tuslerRisks.responsive: Switch to paper cards if needed.

tuslerRisks.mitigation: Give quick hints for common small mistakes.
tuslerRisks.responsive: Show corrective feedback after the turn.

tuslerRisks.mitigation: Log minor interface issues and fix them after the session.

state.facilitatorRole: The facilitator explains the rules, controls the pace, watches the event log, and turns mistakes into debrief questions.
state.wf_dash: Dashboard: top shows round, timer, budget, and health. Centre shows the risk card and heat map. Right side shows the event log. Bottom has response buttons.
state.wf_asset: Risk card: top shows title and category. Middle shows likelihood, impact, and trigger. Bottom shows preventive and responsive actions.
state.wf_portfolio: Portfolio: tabs show decisions, event logs, reflections, KPI evidence, and the final risk register. Export creates a simple report.
state.inScope: In scope are risk cards, classification, budget choices, event logs, debrief reports, and the compassion model with losePoints=0 and no punitive failure.
state.outScope: Out of scope are real-time multiplayer, Jira integration, VR, real-money rewards, and long-term storage of private student data.
state.whyMotivation: The game gives students choice, quick feedback, visible consequences, and a clear reason to discuss their decisions.
state.howEthics: The design uses consent, pseudonymised logs, GDPR/KVKK-aware handling, accessible UI, and non-punitive feedback.
